title: AND, OR and NOT: combining tests

docs.syntax: =AND(test1, test2, ...) needs every test; =OR(...) needs one; =NOT(test) flips it
docs.explain: A single comparison answers one question, and most decisions ask several at once. AND joins tests and answers TRUE only when all of them hold; OR answers TRUE when any one of them does; NOT flips a single logical value. All three take logical tests rather than numbers, so each argument is a comparison — a bare number is treated as TRUE when it is not zero, which is a quiet way to write a test that always passes. In this drill the stock list has a total of 150 and a smallest item of 18 units, so =AND(B8>100,MIN(B2:B7)>=15) is TRUE while OR with the same two tests is also TRUE, which is exactly why picking the wrong one changes nothing on this data and everything on the next sheet. The second screen asks whether any item is under 20 or the total is over 200: the first test is already TRUE, so the answer is TRUE. The usual mistake is reaching for AND when the question says or, and the second is testing an empty column because the range was typed rather than read.
